241.quote_or_event: “Compassion is wealth, want of compassion useless.”
241.explanation: In the Nasihat Nama (Instruction), which Macauliffe records as uttered by Guru Nanak to Mian Mitha, compassion is set among other virtues as the true wealth.
241.tie_back: The Kural calls the wealth of compassion the wealth of all wealths, and this line says simply that compassion is wealth and its absence worthless.
241.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter X, p. 129 (Nasihat Nama)
241._accuracy_note: The wording is close to a one-to-one match, but Macauliffe himself notes that the Nasihat Nama is not found in the Granth Sahib, so it is not scripture and its attribution is uncertain.

242.quote_or_event: “Be kind to all beings-this is more meritorious than bathing at the sixty-eight sacred shrines of pilgrimage and the giving of charity.”
242.explanation: In the Baarah Maah of Raag Maajh Guru Arjan weighs kindness to living beings against the most valued religious acts, pilgrimage and charity, and finds kindness greater.
242.tie_back: The Kural says that however many paths one examines, compassion proves the only true support; Guru Arjan likewise sets compassion above all the other recognised forms of merit.
242.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Raag Maajh, Baarah Maah, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
242._accuracy_note: Strong fit: both rank compassion above the alternatives after comparison, though Guru Arjan's comparison is with ritual merit rather than with every method of inquiry.

243.quote_or_event: “Where there is awesome and terrible heat and blazing sunshine, there, the Name of the Lord will give you shade.”
243.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan promises that in the terrifying passages after death the Name of God will shelter the soul.
243.tie_back: The Kural says those filled with compassion never enter the dark world of suffering; the nearest Sikh assurance is that the Name shields the soul in that fearful realm.
243.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 2, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
243._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both promise protection from a realm of suffering, but Gurbani credits the Name rather than compassion as the shelter.

244.quote_or_event: “They are kind to all beings; they have overpowered the five thieves.”
244.explanation: In the Salok Sahaskriti Guru Arjan describes the holy as those who are kind to every living being and have mastered the five passions.
244.tie_back: The Kural praises those who cherish all living beings and so need not fear the consequences of their deeds; Guru Arjan joins universal kindness with victory over the inner thieves that produce wrongdoing.
244.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1357, Salok Sahaskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
244._accuracy_note: Reasonable: universal kindness is matched directly, and mastery of the five thieves loosely parallels freedom from fearing one's own deeds, but active protection of life is not spelled out.

245.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
245.explanation: Japji reinterprets the myth of the bull that bears the world: what really holds up the earth is dharma, born of compassion.
245.tie_back: Valluvar calls the wind-swept earth to witness that the compassionate do not suffer; Guru Nanak goes further and makes compassion, through dharma, the very support of the earth.
245.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
245._accuracy_note: Reasonable: both join compassion and the earth, but Japji makes compassion the earth's support rather than claiming the compassionate are spared sorrow; the verse is also used in an earlier chapter of this edition.

246.quote_or_event: “The Creation is in the Creator, and the Creator is in the Creation, totally pervading and permeating all places.”
246.explanation: Bhagat Kabir teaches that God dwells in all creatures and all creatures dwell in God.
246.tie_back: The Kural says those who abandon compassion and do wrong have lost sight of life's true purpose; Kabir supplies the Sikh reason such cruelty is a forgetting, since the one harmed carries the same divine presence.
246.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
246._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the verse gives the ground of compassion but does not speak of the pitiless forgetting their own sufferings, which is the Kural's specific charge.

247.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, to use force is tyranny, even if you call it legal. When your account is called for in the Court of the Lord, what will your condition be then?”
247.explanation: Kabir warns that oppression remains tyranny whatever justification it is given, and that it will be judged in the divine court.
247.tie_back: The Kural says the other world holds nothing for those without compassion; Kabir asks what will become of the pitiless when their account is called for hereafter.
247.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir 187 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
247._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the fate of the merciless in the hereafter, though Kabir's target is the forceful killing of animals justified as lawful, and the Kural's matching half about poverty in this world is absent.

248.quote_or_event: “How can anyone know the pain of another, if there is no compassion and sympathy within? The discarded bride is miserable, and loses both worlds”
248.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas says that one with no feeling within cannot know another's pain, and that such a soul loses both this world and the next.
248.tie_back: The Kural says those who have lost compassion are truly destitute and seldom recover; Ravidas likewise describes the heart without sympathy as wretched and bereft in both worlds.
248.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 793, Raag Soohee, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
248._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the translation explicitly links lack of compassion to losing both worlds, although in context the 'pain' is also the soul's longing for God and the hymn does not stress how rare recovery is.

249.quote_or_event: “You kill living beings, and call it a righteous action. Tell me, brother, what would you call an unrighteous action?”
249.explanation: Kabir challenges those who sacrifice animals and call it dharma, asking what could count as sin if that is righteousness.
249.tie_back: Valluvar says the virtue of someone without compassion is no more real than a muddled mind's claim to have seen truth; Kabir likewise exposes religious acts done without compassion as false righteousness.
249.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
249._accuracy_note: Close fit: both deny that dharma practised without compassion is real dharma, with Kabir's example being ritual killing.

250.quote_or_event: “But if a powerful tiger attacks a flock of sheep and kills them, then its master must answer for it.”
250.explanation: In a hymn on Babar's invasion Guru Nanak contrasts fights between equals with the strong falling on the defenceless, which the Lord who owns the flock must answer for.
250.tie_back: The Kural asks the powerful to remember their own fear before the stronger when they move against the weak; Guru Nanak likewise singles out the attack of the strong on the defenceless as the wrong that calls for an account.
250.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 360, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
250._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong on the ethics of the strong against the weak, but Guru Nanak's appeal is to divine accountability rather than to the aggressor's memory of his own fear.
